body: On a Tuesday morning in an empty parish church a man is kneeling on a cushion inside the organ case with a wedge of felt in his teeth. He has been doing this since half past eight. He damps one pipe, holds a key down, and listens to the beats slow and slow and stop. Then the next one. There are eight hundred and something pipes in this instrument and he will be here until four. At about eleven he sits on the bench and plays sixteen bars of a hymn tune to hear how it is all sitting together, and it is the first music made in that building in six days. Nobody is in. He stops in the middle of a phrase and goes back to the felt.
There was worship in that building at eleven o’clock, or there was not, and the question does not turn on anything the organ was doing. It cannot have been the organ. Nobody has ever thought it was.

The question about these tools comes up fast and it deserves a straight answer rather than a clever one. No. A model does not love Yahuah. It does not repent, it cannot mean a word it produces, and nothing it generates is in itself an act of praise.

That should be said without wriggling, because most writing on this subject goes soft exactly here. It is tempting to reach for something about mystery, or about how we cannot really know what goes on inside a machine, and both moves are evasions. The honest position is plainer. Whatever is happening inside a model when it produces a line about the faithfulness of God, it is not the thing that happens inside a person who has found God faithful and says so. There is no inner life to which the words correspond. There is no one there to mean them.

This band does not pretend otherwise anywhere on it. The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 across 121 stations, and the technology behind the music and the voices is stated in the open rather than tucked into a footnote somebody has to go looking for.

Saying so costs something, and it is worth being clear about what. There is a version of this ministry that simply never mentions it, lets listeners assume what they will, and is measurably more comfortable to run. Plenty of people would prefer that version and some of them will leave over the other one. The reason for not taking it is that a ministry which will not be straight about how it works has already surrendered the thing it came to protect, and no amount of good music afterwards buys that back.

But look at what the objection quietly assumes — that the instrument was supposed to be the one doing the worshipping. A pipe organ does not worship. A hymnal does not worship; it is glue and paper and somebody else’s theology. A transmitter has never once meant a word it carried, and the man who pressed the vinyl was thinking about the press. The organ does not worship either, and nobody has ever thought that was an argument against organs, because everybody understood perfectly well where the worship was actually happening.

The dial is arranged around that assumption from end to end. Stations are grouped by what a listener might need at a given hour — the worship formats together, teaching and prayer in their own stretch, the family frequencies where a parent can find them, the international stations in the languages they are sung in. Every one of those groupings is a judgement about a person in a room. None of them is a judgement about the equipment, which is exactly the right way round.
So the interesting question is not the one that gets asked. It is the one underneath it.

Give the objection its due, because there is something real in it. When a congregation sings, the singing is not only aimed at God; it is evidence to the people in the next pew that somebody means it. A recording made by no one supplies none of that. There is no witness in it. And a person who suspects everything they hear was produced by a machine may end up unable to take any of it seriously, which is a genuine loss and not a small one. But notice that this is a worry about the listener’s confidence, not about the machine’s soul. It is a question of whether the words are true and whether they can be checked — and that question, unlike the first one, has an answer.
Worship happens in the person, or it does not happen at all.

At four in the morning a man is walking a hallway with a six-week-old over his shoulder, doing the turn at the end by the airing cupboard and starting back. This is the fourth night. His wife has managed two hours and he is not going to wake her. There is a station on very low on the shelf, the ambient sort, mostly strings and a voice a long way back, and he has chosen nothing about it. Somewhere around the eighth or ninth lap a line about the God who does not sleep goes past, and he says something back to it — not out loud, because the baby has just gone heavy on his shoulder, but he says it. Then he does another eleven laps and puts her down at ten past five.
A machine did not worship in that hallway. A tired man did, once, in the middle of a sentence he did not write, using words he would never have found on his own at four in the morning.

Now the part that has to be conceded. A song made this way carries no testimony behind it, and testimony is not decoration. When you learn that a hymn was written by a man who had just lost his daughters, the hymn changes; you are no longer only reading a claim, you are watching somebody make it under load. There is none of that here and there is no way to manufacture it. Anyone who says the difference does not matter is not being serious about what music has always done for people.

But that loss is a loss of one kind of evidence, not of the thing being sung about. The proper test was never whether the instrument believed. It is whether what comes out of it is true, and whether it puts a person in front of the living God — which is a question about the words and the Scripture underneath them, and can actually be answered by anybody willing to go and look. Every track on this band stands on a passage, and the passage travels with it. The testimony is not missing. It is simply older, and it belongs to people who paid a great deal more for it than any songwriter has.

So the failure mode worth guarding against was never a machine that cannot worship. It is a song that is doctrinally empty and emotionally effective, and human beings have been producing those in enormous quantities for a very long time without any help at all. Sincerity is not the safeguard people think it is. A man can mean every word of something that is not true, and sing it beautifully, and a room can be moved by it, and nothing whatever has been given to anybody.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there. There is music, which is most of the band — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. Every one of them is arranged around a listener rather than around a performer, which is the whole of this article in one sentence.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 314.40 — Midnight Praise. It is Celtic and European ambient worship, built for the long night, the overnight watch and the people still awake, and it is where the question this article opened with dissolves fastest. There is no performer in front of you. There is barely a foreground at all. What is left is a room, an hour that is usually unbearable, and words that are either true or not, and you will find out which within twenty minutes of having it on while you walk a hallway or sit up with somebody. That is not the station worshipping. That is you, which is how it was always going to have to work.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an argument won. You are welcome to keep the objection; it is a reasonable one and it has been answered honestly rather than dismissed. Put HM 314.40 on the next night you are up anyway, at the hour when you are least able to be talked into anything, and see what you find yourself saying back. The organ never worshipped either. Somebody in the building did, and that is the only place it has ever happened.
